full_judgment:
2. In WP No. 4116 of 2007 the petitioner on behalf of the Waqf Administrator challenges the order of acquisition of the schedule property by the impugned gazette dated 07-9-2006 by which the property of the Waqf was included in acquisition. A subsequent application was made challenging the acquisition under LA Case No.138/61-62 on the ground that at the relevant time, in the year 1961-62, provisions of section 93A of the Town Improvement Act, 1953 (TI Act, 1953) were not in existence. That application having been allowed, an additional prayer was inserted as A(1) "to show cause as to why the proceedings of LA Case No. 138/61-62 so far as it relates to the petitioner's land should not be declared to have been passed without lawful authority and is of no legal effect." The petitioners have filed numerous affidavits and supplementary affidavits. The sum and substance of these is to the effect that the property belonged to a Waqf Estate, which was created in 1864 and 1877 and, therefore, it could not be the subject matter of acquisition. Moreover, it is claimed that the legal notices issued under the provisions for acquisition were not properly served upon either the Waqf Administrator or the petitioners. It is a further claim of the petitioners in their additional ground taken that section 93A of the TI Act of 1953 was inserted by Ordinance No.LXIX of 1958. The said ordinance of 1958 was repealed by Ordinance No.XXXVII of 1960 and, therefore, after the year 1960 section 93A did not exist in the statute books and any proceeding for acquisition under such law which did not exist has no legal basis. It is further claimed that although apparently in 1963 there was substitution of section 93A by Ordinance No.VI of 1963 that in effect is illegal since there cannot be any substitution of any provisions of law which did not at all exist at the relevant time. 

 5. The claim of the petitioners in both cases is that the land in question belonged to the Ainuddin and Faizunnessa Waqf Estate which was created in the year 1864 and 1877. After 1950, when the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act came into being, the property was taken over by the government and that was challenged in the civil court. The suit was decreed in favour of the plaintiffs claiming the land of the Waqf Estate. The matter went on appeal to the High Court and, thereafter, to the Supreme Court of Pakistan where the plaintiff's claim was established. Before us, initially the respondents claimed that the Waqf deed itself was a forgery and sought to produce a certified copy of another deed No.30 for the year 1864. However, in due course, the learned Deputy Attorney General having produced a number of original volumes for the year 1864, which were in the keeping of the District Registry, it became clear that deed No.30 dated 22.04.1864 is indeed a Waqf deed written in Persian and appears at pages 63-67 of Volume No.1 of 1864. The deed is contained within the volume which records Wills and the particular deed No.30 is a deed of Wakfnamah dated 22.04.1864 which was registered on 25.04.1864. In our mind there is no longer any doubt as to the authenticity of the said Waqf deed. 

 8. The learned DAG further submits that after the notification is published, the right, title and interest of the owners are extinguished and any subsequent preparation of Khatian and payment or rent does not improve the position of the original owners in respect of the acquired land. In support of his contention, he refers to the decision in the cases or Bangladesh Sangbadpatra Parishad (BSP) vs Bangladesh, 43 DLR (AD) 126 and Bangladesh vs Nawab Abdul Malik Jute Mills Ltd. 60 DLR (AD)7.
